claims.text: A thin Ni coating on W particles improves Cu wetting at the W–Cu interface.
Ni coating reduces void formation in spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu composites.
Ni coating reduces phase separation in spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu composites.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites preserve or enhance mechanical durability under irradiation relative to composites made with uncoated W particles.
Conventional processing of W particles or connected W regions in a Cu matrix leads to voids and phase separation.
Applying a thin Ni coating to W particles before spark plasma sintering creates an interfacial layer between W and Cu.
The Ni interfacial layer enhances bonding between W and Cu.
Enhanced W–Cu interfacial bonding promotes densification.
The Ni coating acts as a diffusional bridge at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni coating lowers the W–Cu interfacial energy barrier during sintering.
Lowering the interfacial energy barrier improves Cu infiltration and adhesion to W particles.
Improved Cu infiltration and adhesion minimize void formation and suppress phase separation.
Reduced void formation and phase separation produce a more uniform W–Cu composite with robust thermal and mechanical properties under irradiation.
Ni-coated W–Cu composites have higher thermal conductivity than otherwise identically processed composites made from uncoated W particles.
Spark-plasma-sintered W–Cu composites made with uncoated W particles typically contain voids and phase separation that impair thermal transport.
The proposed effect is applicable when spark plasma sintering maintains Cu in a molten state below its boiling point.
The proposed effect remains applicable under irradiation environments relevant to fusion-reactor joints.
